title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
summary: Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones. Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN. The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post. The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.” Intermittent sending issues DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing , and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes. But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected. For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum : Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered. hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location. Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm , citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon ; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew , and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. title: Panic over cloud capacity is out of hand
summary: I read the recent piece about AWS cloud capacity being “largely sold out” through 2027 , and my first reaction was fairly simple: Well, that’s that. I guess I’ll stop recommending Amazon Web Services to any client looking to host AI workloads. Clearly, the cloud is full. Please take a number. Your GPU will be available sometime after the next presidential election, assuming the data center hamsters are still running. Of course, I suspect I can still log in to the AWS console today and provision some kind of compute for AI workloads. Maybe not a massive, multiyear, hyperscale GPU allocation suitable for training the next frontier model. Maybe not the exact reserved-capacity block a large AI lab wants to lock down through 2028. But that is not the same thing as saying the cloud provider is “sold out.” The AI infrastructure conversation has gone off the rails. Demand is high. Supply is constrained. GPUs are expensive. Power is a problem. Data centers do not magically appear because somebody wrote “AI strategy” on a whiteboard. All of that is true. But “capacity is tight” and “capacity is sold out” are not the same sentence. The confused market Many cloud providers and infrastructure companies seem very eager to tell the market that their AI capacity is committed for years. I understand the motivation. It signals demand. It reassures investors. It tells customers, partners, and Wall Street that the AI boom is real and that everyone wants what they are selling. It is the infrastructure version of a restaurant saying, “We’re booked solid for months.” It sounds impressive. It creates urgency. It also makes people wonder whether they should even bother calling for a reservation. That is the problem. title: SQLQuack: a SQLGlot alternative in Rust that would rather reject your SQL than return the wrong answer
summary: EDIT - The title should say a ' Polyglot fork ' (Polyglot is a SQLGlot inspired transpiler). Can't edit it now unfortunately. Hey guys! I'm the creator of SQLBuild, and for a while I've wanted a more reliable way to run warehouse SQL locally on DuckDB. SQLGlot and Polyglot are both SQL transpilers that have been a major blessing to the community, and some of my projects (this obvs included) wouldn't have been possible without them. However, at least as of today, these libraries both tend to lean toward generating SQL, even if the SQL may not be runnable or may produce and incorrect result in the target dialect. I had the idea for SQLQuack about six months ago, but only recently got around to building it. The idea was to build a fail-closed transpiler that would tell you first of all if it was parseable, second if it would violate a rule (of the souce dialect), and lastly translate it to DuckDB, only if each statement had some sort of supporting evidence for it from a real warehouse recording (e.g. real snowflake recorded result matching DuckDB). Below is an example of what an error might look like in SQLQuack: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id QUALIFY total > 100 $ sqlquack check qualify.sql error[SQ0203]: QUALIFY needs a window function --> qualify.sql:4:1 | 4 | QUALIFY total > 100 | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ QUALIFY is used without a window function in the SELECT list or QUALIFY | = help: move the condition to WHERE or HAVING, or filter on a window function's result The basic goal is to basically create a dataset of all the warehouse / databases and their true behaviours, such that we a have a truly accurate local compiler for all dialects that can be verified with anyone willing to run the recordings.
